points: The Wealden iron industry was based in the Weald of south-eastern England.
The Weald supplied a large share of the bar iron made in England in the 16th century.
The Weald produced most British cannon until about 1770.
Wealden ironmakers obtained ironstone from several local clay beds.
Wealden ironmakers used charcoal made from the area's abundant woodland.
The Wealden iron industry declined as ironmaking shifted from charcoal to coke.
The Weald had no accessible source of the coal needed to make coke.
The iron ore found in the Weald is siderite.
Siderite was commonly called ironstone and historically called 'mine.'
Siderite occurs in patches or bands in the Weald's Cretaceous clays.
Experienced smelters mixed different grades of ore to get better results.
Remains of pre-Roman opencast quarries survive in the Weald.
Remains of Roman opencast quarries survive in the Weald.
Medieval ore extraction in the Weald relied mainly on digging a series of minepits.
Medieval minepits were about five metres across.
Medieval minepits reached depths of up to twelve metres.
Miners winched material out of the pits in baskets suspended from wooden tripods.
Spoil from each new minepit was used to fill the previous one.
Backfilling the minepits reduced damage to the land.
Backfilling the minepits allowed the land to remain in use.
Charcoal had to be made as close as possible to smelting sites.
Charcoal crumbled to dust if carried too far by cart over rough tracks.
Wood fuelled the open fires used to roast ore before smelting.
Pre-roasting broke down lumps or nodules of ore.
Pre-roasting turned the carbonate in the ore into oxide.
Coppicing could provide a sustainable supply of wood.
To supply a post-medieval blast furnace with charcoal sustainably, timber was needed from within a three-mile (4.8-kilometre) radius if a quarter to a third of the surrounding land was wooded.
Forging and finishing iron from bloomeries and blast furnaces required large quantities of charcoal.
Forging and finishing usually took place at a separate site from smelting.
Water power became important when blast furnaces and finery forges were introduced in the late medieval period.
Blast furnaces needed to run continuously for as long as possible.
A series of ponds in a valley often maintained a steady flow of water to a furnace's waterwheel.
A blast furnace's production run was called a campaign.
A typical campaign lasted from October until late spring.
Campaigns usually ended in late spring because streams began drying up.
Lamberhurst Furnace ran continuously for more than three years in the 1740s.
The River Teise supplied water power to Lamberhurst Furnace.
A finery forge used three or four waterwheels to drive its machinery.
A finery forge could need more water at times than a blast furnace.
A finery forge depended less on a continuous water supply than a blast furnace did.
When a finery forge and a furnace shared a valley, the forge was usually downstream.
Ironworks ponds were formed by damming valleys in the hilly Wealden landscape.
The dam that formed an ironworks pond was called a pond bay.
A pond bay often served as a road.
During a drought in 1754, one furnace manager considered hiring workers to turn the wheel like a treadmill.
The need for continuous water power encouraged development of the water-returning engine.
A water-returning engine used a steam-driven pump to raise water to drive a waterwheel.
About two dozen known Wealden sites produced iron before the Roman invasion.
Most known pre-Roman ironmaking sites are scattered across East Sussex and the Vale of Kent.
The large site at Broadfield in Crawley is the westernmost confirmed smelting site from the pre-Roman period.
There may have been a smelting site associated with an Iron Age enclosure at Piper's Copse near Northchapel in the western Weald.
Pottery styles persisted from the Iron Age into the early Roman period, making it hard to tell whether many sites predate the Roman conquest.
Radiocarbon dating placed the Cullinghurst Wood site at Hartfield between 750 and 350 BC.
Julius Caesar invaded Britain in 55 and 54 BC.
Caesar noted iron production near the coast during his invasions.
Caesar may have been referring to known sites at Sedlescombe and Crowhurst Park near Hastings.
The Romans made extensive use of the Weald's brown and ochre ironstone.
Many Roman roads in the Weald were used to transport iron ore.
Many Roman roads in the Weald were surfaced with slag from iron smelting.
About 113 Roman bloomery sites have been identified in the Weald.
Most of the identified Roman bloomery sites are in East Sussex.
The Weald was one of the most important iron-producing regions in Roman Britain.
Tiles belonging to the Roman fleet known as the Classis Britannica were found at a few ironmaking sites.
The tiles suggest that the Roman fleet either ran those ironworks or obtained iron from them.
Roman-period iron production in the Weald has been estimated at 750 tons a year.
Estimated iron production fell below 200 tons a year after AD 250.
Anglo-Saxon invasion and settlement appear to have ended the Romano-British iron industry in the Weald.
No evidence of Wealden iron smelting has been found between the end of Roman rule and the ninth century.
A primitive bloomery was built at Millbrook on Ashdown Forest in the ninth century.
A small hearth near the Millbrook bloomery was used to reheat iron blooms.
The Millbrook site was dated by radiocarbon and archaeomagnetic methods.
The Millbrook bloomery used technology similar to that of a slightly older furnace excavated in the eastern Netherlands.
The comparison with the Dutch furnace suggests that Romano-British ironmaking methods had been completely lost and replaced by Saxon methods.
There is evidence that iron blooms were forged in settlements near the South Downs.
The forging evidence suggests that other smelting sites may remain undiscovered.
Settlements along the South Downs commonly held outlying land in the Weald for summer grazing.
Smelting may have taken place in the Weald during the summer.
Iron blooms may have been taken back to the main settlements to be worked in winter.
About 30 medieval bloomery sites without water power are known in the Weald.
Most known unpowered medieval bloomery sites in the Weald have not been dated.
Tudeley near Tonbridge is the only unpowered medieval bloomery in the Weald for which operating records survive.
The surviving Tudeley records date to the mid-14th century.
Water power began to be used at Wealden bloomeries around the 14th century.
Fewer than ten water-powered bloomery sites are suspected in the Weald.
The new ironmaking process was devised in the Namur region of present-day Belgium in the 15th century.
The new process spread from Namur to the Pays de Bray on the eastern edge of Normandy before reaching the Weald.
The new ironmaking process used a blast furnace and a finery forge.
The first recorded Wealden blast furnace was at Queenstock in Buxted parish, where the new process was introduced around 1490.
The number of Wealden ironworks increased greatly from around 1540.
Nearly 180 Wealden sites had a blast furnace, a finery forge, or both between the 15th and 18th centuries.
Water power operated the bellows in blast furnaces.
Water power operated the bellows in finery forges.
Water power operated the helve hammers in finery forges.
Dozens of old ironworks ponds survive across the Weald, including ponds still called Furnace Pond or Hammer Pond.
Wealden iron was used to make household utensils.
Wealden iron was used to make nails.
Wealden iron was used to make hinges.
The industry reached its peak toward the end of Elizabeth I's reign.
Most Wealden ironworks were small.
One ironmaster at Brenchley employed 200 men.
Most of the Brenchley ironmaster's workers probably mined ore or cut wood for charcoal.
The ironworks itself needed only a small workforce.
Henry VIII's wars increased demand for armaments.
The Weald became a centre of armaments production in response to increased demand during Henry VIII's reign.
Cast-iron cannon production in the Weald began in 1543.
Ralf Hogge of Buxted cast the first iron cannon.
Hogge's employer was a Sussex vicar.
The vicar who employed Hogge made gunstones for the king.
The Weald was a major supplier of iron to London manufacturers in the 16th and early 17th centuries.
Wealden iron output peaked at more than 9,000 tons a year in the 1590s.
After 1650, Wealden production focused increasingly on cannon.
After 1650, Wealden bar iron was produced only for local use.
The decline of the Weald's London market may have begun in the 1610s, when ironware from the Midlands went on sale there.
Large quantities of Swedish iron were imported after the Restoration.
Wealden bar iron appears to have been unable to compete in London once large quantities of Swedish iron were imported.
Cannon production remained a major Wealden activity until the end of the Seven Years' War.
The Board of Ordnance cut the price it paid for cannon.
The Board of Ordnance's price cut drove several Wealden ironmasters into bankruptcy.
Wealden ironmasters could not match the much lower price accepted by the Scottish Carron Company.
The Carron Company used coke as fuel.
A few Wealden ironworks continued operating on a very small scale after the industry declined.
The forge at Ashburnham was the last Wealden ironworks to close.
Little remains of the furnace and forge buildings.
Steel production was never widespread in the Weald.
Most high-quality steel was imported from Spain, the Middle East, or Germany.
A steel forge was built around 1505 upstream from Newbridge Furnace on Ashdown Forest.
The steel forge upstream from Newbridge Furnace had stopped producing steel by 1539.
The Sydney family produced steel at its mills at Robertsbridge forge and at Sandhurst in Kent.
The Sydney family employed skilled German workers to make steel.
The Sydney family's steel faced strong competition from German suppliers.
A steel forge operated at Warbleton in Sussex in the 17th century.
Lamberhurst Foundry is believed to have made cast-iron railings for St Paul's Cathedral between 1710 and 1714.
The St Paul's railings were among the earliest cast-iron railings made in England.
Christopher Wren did not want a fence around St Paul's Cathedral.
If a fence had to be installed, Wren preferred wrought iron to cast iron.
The railings surrounded St Paul's Cathedral.
The railings incorporated seven gates.
The railings weighed 200 tons.
The railings cost six pence per pound.
The railings cost £11,202 in total.
No later railings are known to have been cast in the Weald.
Cambridge Senate House was another early site to use cast-iron railings.
St Martin-in-the-Fields in London was another early site to use cast-iron railings.

question.text: What materials did the Wealden iron industry use?
quotes: using local ironstone and charcoal made from woodland
used local ironstone, charcoal from coppiced woodland
